title: Westpac: 70pc of employees use AI daily
full_text:
Westpac has told investors artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping how its customers and employees interact with the bank, and sees little chance this will slow down as the cost of using the tools continues to fall.
In a strategy briefing held just days after Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for a "worldwide pacing of the frontier" of AI to avoid serious risk, Westpac said more than 95 per cent of its 35,000 employees were using the tools at least monthly, up from 69 per cent at the start of the year.
More than 70 per cent had built AI tools into their everyday work, compared with 14 per cent in January, the bank said in an investor presentation.
"We're in the midst of one of the most significant shifts our industry has ever seen," said Andrew McMullen, Westpac's chief data, digital and AI officer.
"The ability to understand, to reason and act on information is becoming dramatically cheaper and much more accessible. That doesn't just improve existing processes; it changes what we do, how quickly we can do it, and what customers have now come to expect of us," he told the briefing.
Australia's four major banks have been among the most rapid adopters of AI tools, hoping to improve customer service and save money.
In August, Commonwealth Bank said its investment in the technology was beginning to pay for itself, with what it described as gross benefits increasing to $200 million in the year to June 30 and heading to $400 million.
Speaking at the bank's results presentation, chief executive Matt Comyn said AI had improved business banker productivity by 29 per cent and led to 64 per cent more technology changes being deployed.
Westpac told investors on Tuesday that the use of AI had increased the productivity of teams writing software code by 35 per cent. Another project - migrating St George customers to Westpac platforms - had been accelerated by two years with the new tools.
In other parts of the bank, Westpac said autonomous agents used in the mortgages and consumer finance division had reduced errors 42 per cent and removed about 250,000 manual activities every year, saving 150,000 hours of work. In home lending, the technology had resulted in a 35 per cent lift in loan approval volumes in the bank's proprietary channel.
Dan Jermyn, Westpac's chief AI officer, said worries raised by Amodei and others showed "common recognition of the fact that we need to be very thoughtful about the development of AI", but did not mean a limited number of large language models developers should control the debate.
Jermyn said Westpac was also forced to be "very thoughtful" about AI because of the cost of usage, or tokens, compared with returns.
"We're seeing an increase in the number of tokens being used. But actually, the unit economics ... is continually being squeezed as well. So they're actually progressing broadly at the same kind of rate," he added.
In response to questions from analysts, Jermyn pointed to one project to migrate an internal system that would typically cost a low seven-figure sum and take a year to complete. Instead, the move was finalised with $US12,000 ($17,000) in tokens. "The return on investment there is very clear," he said.
Jarden analyst Matt Wilson said: "Hamstrung by complex, fragmented legacy ... architecture and layers of bureaucracy, banks should be able to harness new tech to harvest efficiency dividends from streamlined processes, redesigned value chains, improved controls and faster decision-making."
He warned, however, that pressure on revenues could grow as new players disrupted "a dated business model based on bundling, complexity".
There are also growing concerns about risks from the increasing reliance on AI - even if the models being employed are not cutting edge.
Speaking at The Australian Financial Review Asia Summit on Tuesday, ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos said it was "becoming obvious [that] if you don't have enough guardrails and limitations, AI will do a lot of rogue things".
Fears about the ability to control AI have grown since an OpenAI model broke out of its testing environment and hacked another company. This month, an Anthropic researcher quit and warned that under the worst-case scenario, "by the end of next year things could be out of control already".
The biggest worry for companies, however, is the likelihood that automated models will misuse data or hallucinate responses. Westpac has already switched on a platform called Adapt to manage AI governance.
Lawyers say governing AI will remain a big challenge for banks, and Amodei's warning about the "risk of losing control of AI systems" would raise concerns for financial regulators.
"Regulated firms will not stand still because it is a highly competitive market of narrow margins," said Fiona Ghosh, a London-based partner of Ashurst Perkins Coie.
"When you're procuring systems from entities determining their own risks, and you are not in a position to necessarily assess those, that will be of concern to a regulator. The major concern is how do you build adaptability into your governance model."
